question: This nonsense word stayed live in a tweet for more than six hours before being deleted. It capped off a message reading in part "despite the constant negative press," posted by Donald Trump just after midnight on May 31st, 2017. Both Merriam-Webster's and Oxford Dictionaries' social media accounts jokingly weighed in on its supposed definition once it became the world's top trending hashtag. Congressional staffers later riffed on the typo in the name of a tongue-in-cheek bill concerning presidential social media archives. Widely assumed to be a botched attempt at typing "coverage," it prompted its author to tweet the next morning, inviting followers to "figure out the true meaning" of the term. For 10 points, name this nonsense word from a viral 2017 presidential Twitter typo.

In this visual novel, the protagonist is the only human student enrolled at a high school otherwise populated entirely by birds. Its title puns on the Japanese word for pigeon alongside the English words for "heartfelt" and "hurtful." Originally released in Japan in 2011 for Windows and OS X, it offers up to eight potential avian partners, including several pigeons, quails, and doves, with each route lasting thirty to sixty minutes. Despite its absurd premise, critics and players praised its surprisingly dark and emotionally serious narrative, and it holds an approval rating of 94 percent among user reviews on Steam. For 10 points, name this dating simulator whose love interests are all birds.

In December 2018, actor Will Smith appeared in a widely mocked annual best-of compilation released by a major video-sharing platform, cheerfully using this exclamation to introduce a segment revisiting old footage. The clip quickly became a stand-alone reaction sound bite, endlessly recut into unrelated videos and captions. That year's edition of the platform's retrospective was panned for its try-hard attempts to reference trending memes and creators, making Smith's enthusiastic delivery an ironic highlight. Compilations of the clip continue to circulate as a sarcastic segue whenever old content resurfaces online. For 10 points, give this exclamation that Will Smith used to introduce a look back at old clips.

This four-letter internet abbreviation labels a video genre in which a creator narrates their morning routine, often while applying makeup or choosing an outfit, directly to camera. Though the format traces back to a 2011 YouTube video by beauty vlogger Shaaanxo, it exploded into a dominant TikTok trend during the 2020s. By 2023, its hashtag had accumulated more than 165 billion views on that platform, with roughly 100 billion added in just the preceding year. For 10 points, give this abbreviation for the phrase "get ready with me".

This two-part catchphrase, describing how its creator carries herself at work, went viral on TikTok in August 2024, its original video eventually racking up more than 57 million views. Jennifer Lopez, RuPaul, and Joe Jonas were among the celebrities who recorded their own clips using its audio. Dictionary.com later named the phrase its word of the year. A man in Washington state attempted to trademark the expression before its creator, Jools Lebron, could capitalize on it herself. Lebron later said the sudden fame "ruined her life" and contributed to a struggle with substance abuse. For 10 points, give this two-adjective phrase in which a TikToker describes herself as thoughtful and reserved at the office.
answer: very mindful, very demure [or very demure, very mindful; prompt on mindful; prompt on demure]

question: This dismissive two-word retort tells someone that their unsolicited opinion or overshare wasn't wanted. A subreddit devoted to showcasing people who over-explained things without being prompted was founded in September 2017. The retort gained wider traction as a reaction-image format between 2019 and 2020, building on an earlier 2018 Twitter-joke format that mocked people for volunteering opinions no one wanted, framed as though quoting a nonexistent speaker. The full expression had circulated informally online for years before its meme-ified breakout. For 10 points, give this two-word rejoinder telling someone their comment was unsolicited.

This three-letter slang term was coined in the 1980s to describe women involved in certain Asian American gang subcultures. Its associated look and attitude developed in the 1990s among Chinese American communities in New York City and Vietnamese American communities in Southern California, framed by scholars as a deliberate rebellion against the "model minority" stereotype. Unlike labels imposed from outside their communities, this identity was created by the young women who embodied it. In the 2010s and 2020s, it evolved into a mainstream beauty and fashion aesthetic popularized on Instagram and TikTok, often featuring dyed or ombre hair and bold eyeliner. For 10 points, give this abbreviation that stands for "Asian Baby Girl".

According to fandom historian Fred Patten, this fandom's roots trace to a 1980 science-fiction convention, where a drawing from Steve Gallacci's comic "Albedo Anthropomorphics" sparked a discussion group about anthropomorphic characters. The community's name for itself appeared in fanzines as early as 1983. Its first dedicated gathering, ConFurence Zero, was held in 1989, and the community grew further through the Usenet newsgroup alt.fan.furry during the 1990s. Members create and enjoy art and costumes ("fursuits") featuring anthropomorphic animal characters, and now gather at large annual conventions. For 10 points, name this fandom for anthropomorphic animal enthusiasts.

A comedic video uploaded to a Kenyan news outlet's Facebook page on November 24th, 2016, carried the title "This Man Has the Hardest Name in Africa." In the clip, an interviewer asks the subject for his name, only to be met with this deliberately exaggerated, tongue-twisting mouthful, playing on the tradition of long personal names in Nigeria's Edo region. The name is not the man's real one; it was invented purely for comic effect. The clip spawned countless remixes and pronunciation-challenge spinoffs across YouTube and TikTok, and was later referenced by British YouTuber KSI. For 10 points, give this comically long, invented name from a viral fake interview clip.

This three-word rejoinder is typically appended, in italics, after a deliberately implausible or undesirable statement to underscore how nobody would actually say such a thing. Searches for the phrase began climbing in January 2012, and a Tumblr blog collecting examples launched that same month, followed by a Twitter account in March. A widely cited theory traces its roots to an earlier meme series mocking overused expressions, spun off into a variant about things a specific group would never say. By March 2013, the standalone phrase had already racked up more than 91,000 uses across social media. For 10 points, give this sarcastic three-word phrase appended to mock a statement that nobody would sincerely make.

This rage comic character's bald, moon-shaped head, scrunched lips, and bulging bloodshot eyes were drawn by illustrator May Oswald in under fifteen minutes in early 2010. She uploaded the image to 4chan and Reddit on March 18th of that year. Its two-word Spanish caption, translating to "I like it," originally accompanied reaction images depicting an odd sense of pleasure in deliberately awkward or perverse situations, though usage later broadened to describe any moment of being disturbed and delighted at once. Years later, an NFT scammer stole Oswald's identity while trying to profit off the character she created. For 10 points, name this bald, bug-eyed rage comic character whose two-word Spanish caption expresses approval of something odd or unsettling.

A 2005 episode of the surreal MTV adult sketch show "Wonder Showzen" included a faux public-service announcement about tolerance that instead deployed a barrage of shockingly offensive ethnic stereotype jokes as satire. Viewers unfamiliar with the source often mistake the clip for a genuine, embarrassingly dated PSA that "could never air today". Its singsong refrain about togetherness resurfaced as an ironic catchphrase on TikTok around 2020 and 2021. A 2021 reaction video, whose title promised to stop playback the moment something racist was heard, gained over 1.2 million views in under two months. For 10 points, give this darkly satirical refrain about embracing diversity, taken from a segment on an early-2000s sketch show.
answer: we gotta celebrate our differences [or we've got to celebrate our differences]

question: This five-letter YouTube abbreviation debuted as a segment on June 22nd, 2017, in which PewDiePie reacts to memes his subscribers had posted to Reddit in response to a weekly prompt. It was conceived as a parody of fellow YouTuber Jacksfilms's own recurring series asking a similar question about the previous day rather than the previous week. In 2021, the segment was folded into a broader Friday-upload franchise. For 10 points, give this abbreviation, standing for "Last Week I Asked You".

This recurring internet-video segment debuted on November 23rd, 2017, and opens with its host's signature double hand-clap. A running joke holds that any joke image showcased on the show is thereby rendered "dead," since it has now reached mainstream saturation. In February 2019, tech billionaire Elon Musk appeared as a guest co-host in a stunt tied to its creator's subscriber-count race against an Indian record label, and other guests included commentator Ben Shapiro and television psychologist Dr. Phil. The series wound down after 2019 as its host shifted focus to other content. For 10 points, name this joke-critiquing segment hosted by PewDiePie.

A YouTube video-title fad that began in October 2008 dared viewers to watch a clip without cracking a smile. On October 6th of that year, a user named Gmaerking310 uploaded a looping video of a dancing Stormtrooper with a title daring viewers not to crack up. It is unclear whether this fad grew independently or descended from a similarly themed 4chan format that penalized anyone who broke composure first. The format exploded into one of YouTube's most durable video genres, spawning endless themed compilations daring viewers to keep a straight face. For 10 points, name this video-title format and viewer dare, often paired with compilations of memes or bloopers.
answer: try not to laugh challenge [or try not to laugh or grin]

question: This 2012 animated public-safety campaign was commissioned by Metro Trains in Melbourne, Australia, and produced by ad agency McCann Melbourne with Steven Page, with animation by Julian Frost. Its earworm theme song, featuring a parade of cartoon characters meeting darkly comic and preventable fates, reached the top ten on iTunes within 24 hours of release and hit number one in 28 countries. A companion mobile game was released alongside it, and Metro Trains reported a 21 percent drop in station-related incidents after the campaign launched. Its central video has drawn more than 340 million views on YouTube. For 10 points, name this Australian rail-safety campaign whose title suggests foolish methods of meeting one's end.

This rapid, bent-knee hip-shaking dance move emerged from the New Orleans bounce music scene of the late 1980s. Its name is believed to have first appeared on record in DJ Jubilee's 1993 single "Do the Jubilee All," and exposure widened nationally after the Ying Yang Twins released a hit single referencing the move in its title in 2000. Web searches for the term began climbing in November 2011, and it was formally added to Oxford Dictionaries Online in 2013, an addition widely, if imprecisely, credited to a headline-grabbing performance by Miley Cyrus alongside Robin Thicke at that year's MTV Video Music Awards. For 10 points, name this dance move, rooted in New Orleans bounce culture, that involves rapidly shaking one's hips and rear while squatting.

This lyric appears in "Revenge," a 2011 parody of Usher's "DJ Got Us Fallin' in Love" about a hostile in-game mob, released on August 19th of that year by YouTuber CaptainSparklez. Although the song's official lyric sheet reportedly prints a different, more formal interjection, its performer confirmed that what listeners actually hear sung is this more casual phrasing. Nearly a decade after its release, the song saw a nostalgic meme resurgence in 2019. Fans on the messaging platform Discord later turned its full lyrics into a group game, in which members type out the song line by line in order and must start over from the beginning if anyone makes a mistake. For 10 points, give this expression of resigned annoyance about a hostile, hissing Minecraft mob, sung at the start of a parody song's chorus.

This low-budget Chinese animated film follows a cowardly bovine protagonist who must navigate a dreamscape to learn courage. It was shipped to Chinese theaters without an official poster, forcing some theater employees to draw their own promotional art. After flopping in its opening week, the film was rescued by social media users who mockingly celebrated its amateurish animation, turning it into a "so bad it's good" phenomenon compared to the ironic fandom around the 2022 film "Morbius". An English-subtitled version later spread the joke internationally, and the film's notoriety even inspired an unrelated cryptocurrency token launched on the BNB Smart Chain in August 2026. For 10 points, name this animated Chinese flop-turned-meme about a timid cow.
